# Research a scene before generation

Read this module before a new scene master or a substantial scene redesign.
For a narrow edit, reuse the approved scene study and inspect the decisions that change.

## Inspect real references

Start with the reference pages and examples that the user supplied.
Research the scene's real setting, period, architecture, furniture, equipment, and colors.
Prefer original designer portfolios, institutional photographs, and reliable archives.
Open the source pages and visually inspect the photographs.
Do not use search snippets or unviewed images as visual evidence.

Inspect at least five distinct relevant images across different views or real examples.
Use more when the setting or a design decision remains unclear.
Do not count crops or resized copies of one photograph as different references.
One well-documented collection can supply several useful references.
Separate a photograph's capture date from its publication or upload date.

Record source URLs, dates when known, and observed design features in the ignored scene study.
Keep downloaded reference images, raw prompts, and review pages in `tmp/`.
Do not put private research or review galleries in public documentation.
Verified web evidence takes precedence over conflicting private descriptions.

When a moderator has a real-person inspiration, confirm that mapping before generation.
Use the [character identity research procedure](../../generate-character-openai/references/selection-generation.md#research-identity-before-selection-generation).
Inspect at least three distinct usable photographs of the person and target five.
Keep recognizable face and hair traits in the shared drawn style.
Do not substitute a generic face for a researched identity.
Keep real names and reference descriptions out of shipping metadata and public specifications.

## Design a specific, richly furnished scene

Extract a coherent set of architectural forms, materials, furniture, and period equipment.
Give large, medium, and small objects distinct roles in the composition.
Keep enough identifying detail inside the narrow viewport crop.
Do not put all useful set detail in expendable outer strips.
Do not interpret flat cartoon shading as empty walls, sparse furniture, or minimal color.
Show material differences with shape, contour, and authored color regions.
Avoid photographic texture and arbitrary clutter.

Choose a palette for this scene, not one identical palette for every location.
Compare the proposed background with actual roster characters.
Keep their faces, clothing, hands, and signature props separate through value and hue contrast.
Do not put navy-clothed characters against a large navy field without clear separation.
Use quieter detail behind controls and faces, rather than erasing those regions into blank space.
Warm materials are permitted; a global warm filter is not.

Keep the approved editorial-cartoon rendering across people, objects, and architecture.
Reference photographs supply design evidence, not a photographic rendering target.
Make an original composition. Do not copy a complete set, branding, signage, or artwork.

## Prepare the request and review

Write the scene identity, selected palette, object inventory, layer boundaries, and crop requirements.
Assign every attached reference a role: environment, palette, identity, or cartoon rendering.
Use a small representative set of inspected images within the tool's attachment limit.
Keep observations from the broader research in the written brief.
An explicit user reference instruction takes precedence over an older text-only instruction for that task.
Continue to honor unrelated source exclusions and route limits.

Review the candidate with actual approved characters and the appropriate foreground layer.
Check character/background separation, scene richness, researched likeness, and interface clearance.
Keep source-image review, static composition previews, and integrated browser checks distinct.
Record product-owner visual approval separately from unresolved integration checks.
Follow the user's testing boundary. Do not start a quality gate when the user has deferred it.
